items.stem: Why should a presenter define a single core message before building slides?

options.text: It keeps every slide and point aligned to one clear takeaway
options.rationale: Correct: a core message gives the talk focus and prevents overload.

options.text: It means only one slide is allowed
options.rationale: A core message guides many slides; it does not limit slide count.

options.text: It removes the need to know the audience
It guarantees no questions will be asked
options.rationale: A clear message often invites engaged questions.

items.explanation: Correct: a core message gives the talk focus and prevents overload.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which practices make presentation slides more effective? (Select TWO)

options.text: Using slides to support speech rather than duplicate it
options.rationale: Correct: slides should reinforce, not repeat, the spoken message.

options.text: Simplifying charts to show the one point that matters
options.rationale: Correct: a focused visual communicates faster than a cluttered one.

options.text: Filling each slide with dense paragraphs to read aloud
options.rationale: Reading dense text aloud loses the audience.

options.text: Adding every data series available to a chart
options.rationale: Overloaded charts obscure the key insight.

items.explanation: Correct: slides should reinforce, not repeat, the spoken message.

items.stem: A presenter receives a sharp, challenging question. What is the most professional response?

options.text: Treat it as genuine interest and answer calmly and directly
options.rationale: Correct: calm, direct engagement maintains credibility.

options.text: Become defensive and dismiss the questioner
Answer a different, easier question instead
options.rationale: Dodging is transparent and erodes trust.

items.explanation: Correct: calm, direct engagement maintains credibility.
